title: Matthew 23:16–22
context: Jesus continues the woes against casuistry that ranks oaths by gold and gifts while sidelining temple, altar, and God. Blind guides invent loopholes; He restores the sacred order that ends at the throne.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Older voices from both traditions on Matthew 23:16–22.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Whosoever shall swear by the gold - The covetous man, says one, still gives preference to the object of his lust; gold has still the first place in his heart. A man is to be suspected when he recommends those good works most from which he receives most advantage.
arminian.source: Commentary on the New Testament (on Matt 23:16–22)

reformed.quote: Woe to you, blind guides, As ambition is almost always connected with hypocrisy, so the superstitions of the people are usually encouraged by the covetousness and rapacity of pastors. The world has, indeed, a natural propensity to errors, and even draws down upon itself, as if on purpose, every kind of deceit and imposture; but improper modes of worship come to gain a footing only when they are confirmed by the rulers themselves.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 23:16–22)

verses.text: “Woe to you, you blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, he is obligated.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Blind guides invent oath rankings: temple oath “nothing,” gold oath binding. Technical religion excuses broken word.

Classical Arminians find a call to integrity. Grace frees people from loophole ethics; truthfulness before God is not optional theater.
verses.reformedNotes:
Woe on blind guides and their oath casuistry. Gold elevated above the temple reverses God’s order.

False teaching twists holy things into human systems. Christ judges the blindness that leads others by invented rules.

verses.text: You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?
verses.arminianNotes:
Fools miss the obvious: the temple consecrates the gold. Priority belongs to God’s dwelling, not the metal.

They must repent of their clever inversions. God invites renewed sight that honors what He makes sacred.
verses.reformedNotes:
Blind fools—sharp prophetic speech. The temple makes the gold sacred, not the reverse.

God defines holiness. Human valuations that flip His order stand under rebuke.

verses.text: And, ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is on it, he is obligated.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Same pattern with altar and gift. The offering is treated as more binding than the altar that receives it.

Arminian readers warn against religious deals that protect property-language over worship. Grace calls for honest speech without graded escapes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Altar oath dismissed; gift oath enforced. Again the human gift outranks God’s appointed place.

Casuistry serves self-interest. The Lord’s woe strips the cover from manipulative piety.

verses.text: You blind fools! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift?
verses.arminianNotes:
Blind men: the altar makes the gift sacred. Worship’s furniture of God outranks the donor’s present.

Humility returns gifts to their place. God enables clearer seeing when pride’s loopholes are abandoned.
verses.reformedNotes:
The altar consecrates the gift. God’s means of holiness set the rank.

The truth corrects their blindness. Christ restores the grammar of sacredness His opponents scrambled.

verses.text: He therefore who swears by the altar, swears by it and by everything on it.
verses.arminianNotes:
No partial oath: altar includes everything on it. Words before holy things pull the whole into the vow.

Arminian readers urge simple truthfulness (cf. Matt 5:33–37). Grace trains speech that needs no clever carve-outs.
verses.reformedNotes:
Swearing by the altar binds the swearer to altar and contents. Jesus collapses their distinctions.

God’s holiness is indivisible here. The Word exposes fragmented ethics as false.

verses.text: He who swears by the temple, swears by it and by him who has been living in it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Temple oath reaches Him who dwells there. Every religious vow finally faces God Himself.

Take God seriously when you speak. Grace invites reverence that refuses empty formulas.
verses.reformedNotes:
Temple oath is oath by the Dweller. God is the true referent of sacred speech.

The living God inhabits His house by promise. Casuistry that ignores Him is atheism in religious dress.

verses.text: He who swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God and by him who sits on it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Heaven leads to God’s throne and the One seated there. No “safe” oath escapes His presence.

Arminians close the loophole path: all roads of sacred speech end at God. The woe summons repentant integrity under the King.
verses.reformedNotes:
Heaven = throne of God and Him who sits on it. Ultimate accountability is settled.

God’s sovereignty frames every vow. Christ drives ethics back to the enthroned Lord—judgment and truth meet at the throne.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject oath casuistry that sidelines God. Arminians highlight a sincere call to truthful speech and repentant integrity; Reformed readers emphasize God’s throne as the sovereign end of every sacred oath Christ exposes.
